feedback: If a learner predicts the tail should disappear because it only hurts survival: they are treating survival as the whole of fitness. Point to the mating-success curve — more offspring from showier males can outweigh the survival cost.

If a learner says the peacock grows a big tail 'on purpose' to look good: recast it as selection over many generations on heritable variation in tail size via peahen preference, not a choice made within one individual's lifetime.
If a learner picks the smallest tail as 'best': ask them to read the NET curve, not the survival curve alone — the fitness optimum is where mating benefit minus survival cost is greatest.
activities.intendedInsight: Fitness means reproductive success, not survival or strength: a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough. The same logic covers other sexually selected traits (bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls) and both routes to mating success — female choice and male-male competition. Ornaments can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice, not mere decoration.
learnerActions: Vary the size of a peacock's ornament and read off two quantities that change with it: a rising survival cost (slower, easier for predators to catch) and a rising mating success (peahens choose showier males).

Combine the two into a net reproductive-success curve and find where it peaks. With the model's settings, notice the peak can sit at a large, 'wasteful'-looking tail rather than a small survival-safe one.

Increase the strength of female preference and observe how the optimum tail size shifts larger. In runaway selection, the preference and the tail evolve together over generations because offspring inherit both, so this pressure can keep strengthening.

Relate the same cost-versus-mating trade-off to other sexually selected traits — bird-of-paradise courtship displays and loud frog mating calls — and note that the mating advantage can arise through female choice OR through male-male competition.
State in your own words why natural selection has NOT removed the costly tail.
activities.title: Peacock's tail: when a survival cost pays off

feedback: If a learner explains the worker bee's sacrifice as 'for the good of the species': introduce inclusive fitness — helping close relatives propagates shared genes, so the sacrifice favours copies of the helper's own genes carried in kin.
If a learner uses r for distant kin as if it were 0.5: have them check the relatedness value; the lower r shrinks rB and raises the bar for helping to pay off.
If a learner concludes altruism disproves natural selection: show that the rule PREDICTS when helping is favoured, so apparent niceness is consistent with gene-level selection.
activities.intendedInsight: Apparent self-sacrifice toward relatives is a calculable prediction of inclusive fitness: an altruism gene spreads when rB > C. This replaces vague group-benefit reasoning with quantitative individual/gene-level reasoning.
learnerActions: Set a relatedness value r for the helper and the helped (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5), a benefit B to the relative, and a cost C to the helper.
Compute rB and compare it with C; decide whether the altruism gene should spread (rB > C) or die out (rB < C).

Work a model case: treat a meerkat sentinel as paying a cost C to warn relatives (benefit B shared among kin). Vary r, B and C and find the threshold where helping becomes favoured. Note that field studies suggest sentinels may face little extra risk and may also benefit themselves (for example, they often spot danger and reach cover first), so real sentinel behaviour may not be pure kin-selected altruism.
Explain why this is a gene's-eye prediction — helping copies of one's own genes carried in relatives — rather than 'for the good of the species'.
activities.title: Hamilton's rule: why a sterile worker or a sentinel helps

feedback: If a learner expects pure aggression always to win: with injury cost greater than resource value, have them seed a population of almost all hawks plus a few doves (or add a few dove mutants to an all-hawk population) and watch hawks' average payoff fall as they keep fighting each other; the rare doves then do better than the hawks and increase. A population with no doves at all cannot be invaded by doves until some doves appear. (If injury cost is not greater than resource value the balance shifts toward hawks, so the payoffs matter.)

If a learner expects a single best strategy: point to the stable MIX the population converges on under these payoffs, and show how changing the payoffs moves that mix — or tips it to pure hawk — rather than crowning one fixed winner.

If a learner thinks the equilibrium is set by the starting mix: have them try several different starting mixes that each contain both hawks and doves, keeping the payoffs fixed, and notice they converge toward the same stable proportion.
activities.intendedInsight: The best behaviour can be frequency-dependent: with injury cost exceeding resource value an ESS is a stable mix, not a lone winner. 'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest or most aggressive always wins — the best move depends on what everyone else is playing and on the payoff values (with a low injury cost, pure hawk can instead be favoured).
learnerActions: Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and work out what a hawk and a dove each gain when they meet a hawk and when they meet a dove.

Seed a population with a chosen starting mix of hawks and doves and let it play repeated contests. With the default payoffs set so injury cost exceeds resource value, watch the proportions settle toward a stable mixed equilibrium (the evolutionarily stable strategy).

Change the payoffs (e.g. the cost of injury in a hawk-hawk fight) and observe how the equilibrium moves — a mixed ESS when injury cost exceeds resource value, shifting toward pure hawk when it does not.

With injury cost set higher than the resource value, predict what happens when a few doves are added to a population that is almost all hawks, then test it: explain why pure aggression stops winning once almost everyone is a hawk.
activities.title: Hawk-dove game: no single best move

feedback: For a fitness item answered as 'survives longest' or 'strongest': restate fitness as reproductive success and cite the showy short-lived male who out-reproduces a drab survivor.
For an rB-vs-C error: have the learner recompute rB and line it up against C before deciding.
A recognition check confirms recall but does not show whether the learner can explore the trade-offs and equilibria themselves — pair it with the models above.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix as checkable knowledge.
learnerActions: Answer what 'fittest' means in evolution (reproductive success, not longest survival or greatest strength).
Given r, B and C values, compute rB and state whether rB > C, and hence whether helping is favoured.
Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and identify which strategy pays better against a given opponent.
activities.title: Knowledge check: fitness, Hamilton's rule and payoffs

feedback: If a learner settles 'nobility' as fact: ask what observation would distinguish a noble motive from a kin-selected one, and whether either is directly measurable.
If a learner accepts an animal-culture claim uncritically: have them separate the behaviour observed from the inferred inner state, and name the evidence needed.
Keep this as discussion: the quantitative models above are best operated, while this extension builds the working-scientifically skill of constructing evidence-based explanations.
activities.intendedInsight: Behavioural explanations must be evidence-based; cognitive-ethology claims about animal emotion or culture are open evidence questions, and group-benefit language can usually be recast in individual/gene-level terms.
learnerActions: Argue the possible explanations for 'is the meerkat sentinel being noble, is it Hamilton's rule, or is it simply looking after itself?' and decide which explanations make testable predictions.
Examine a claim about animal emotion, play or culture and separate the evidence from the interpretation — state what observation would support or weaken the claim.
Challenge a 'for the good of the species' statement and reframe it at the individual/gene level.
activities.title: Optional debate: noble meerkat, or Hamilton's rule? (cognitive ethology extension)
